summary.text: Acting for Thomas Rowe (claimant), this brief addresses 1 issue(s) arising from Rowe v Skyline Terraces Ltd: Mr Rowe argues that the hire contract was frustrated by the cancellation of the fireworks.
Was the contract frustrated by a supervening event that destroyed its common foundation? Finely balanced for Thomas Rowe.

facts.text: On 10 May 2025 Mr Rowe agreed to hire Skyline's rooftop terrace for the evening of 5 July 2025 for £12,000 and paid a £4,000 deposit.

Skyline's online listing advertised the terrace as "the best view in London of the Thames Victory Fireworks", a display planned to celebrate the city hosting a sporting final. Mr Rowe's emails to Skyline said his guests were coming "to watch the fireworks", and Skyline's reply promised "front-row seats for the display".
The written hire agreement described only "exclusive use of the terrace, 6pm to midnight, with bar service" and did not mention the fireworks.
On 28 June 2025 the council cancelled the fireworks display after a safety review.
The terrace, bar and staff remained available on 5 July 2025. On 29 June 2025 Mr Rowe cancelled his event and asked for his deposit back.

Skyline refuses to return the deposit and claims the £8,000 balance. It says the terrace could still be used, that the fireworks were only Mr Rowe's own commercial purpose, and that the event simply became less attractive.

issues.question: Was the contract frustrated by a supervening event that destroyed its common foundation?

proposition.text: A contract may be frustrated not only by physical impossibility but where a supervening event destroys a state of affairs which both parties regarded as the basis of the contract, even if literal performance remains possible.
Where performance depends on the continued existence of a specific thing, the destruction of that thing without fault discharges the contract.

opposing_precedents.case_name: Davis Contractors Ltd v Fareham Urban District Council

proposition.text: Frustration occurs only where, without default of either party, a contractual obligation has become incapable of being performed because the circumstances would render it a thing radically different from that which was undertaken.

opposing_precedents.case_name: Herne Bay Steam Boat Co v Hutton

proposition.text: Frustration does not apply where the event defeats only one party's purpose or makes the bargain less profitable; the risk of the venture falling short lies on the party who undertook it.

supporting_argument.text: Krell v Henry [1903] 2 KB 740 supports Thomas Rowe on this issue: A contract may be frustrated not only by physical impossibility but where a supervening event destroys a state of affairs which both parties regarded as the basis of the contract, even if literal performance remains possible. That reasoning applies here: On 10 May 2025 Mr Rowe agreed to hire Skyline's rooftop terrace for the evening of 5 July 2025 for £12,000 and paid a £4,000 deposit.

Taylor v Caldwell (1863) 3 B & S 826 supports Thomas Rowe on this issue: Where performance depends on the continued existence of a specific thing, the destruction of that thing without fault discharges the contract. That reasoning applies here: The terrace, bar and staff remained available on 5 July 2025. On 29 June 2025 Mr Rowe cancelled his event and asked for his deposit back.

Davis Contractors Ltd v Fareham Urban District Council is distinguishable on its facts: Contractors agreed to build 78 houses for a fixed price within eight months. By contrast, in this case: The written hire agreement described only "exclusive use of the terrace, 6pm to midnight, with bar service" and did not mention the fireworks.

Herne Bay Steam Boat Co v Hutton is distinguishable on its facts: Hutton chartered a steamboat to take paying passengers to see the naval review at Spithead and to cruise round the fleet. By contrast, in this case: On 28 June 2025 the council cancelled the fireworks display after a safety review.
